opus-5.5.text:
Yes, I think it's an iterative evolution, but each step changes what the model is fundamentally trained to do, so it's more than a simple upgrade.

With chatbots, the core capability was imitation. You pretrain on a huge amount of text, then do instruction tuning and RLHF so the model responds in a way humans like. It's essentially one turn: you ask, it answers. The model is learning to produce a good-looking response, and the feedback is mostly about human preference.

Reasoning models were a real shift, and the key was reinforcement learning. Once you have tasks with verifiable rewards, like math problems or code that passes tests, you can let the model think for a long time, try things, make mistakes, backtrack, and only reward whether the final answer is correct. The model then learns to reason on its own instead of copying the shape of a human answer. That's why you see these long chains of thought where the model says "wait, let me check this again." Nobody wrote that behavior by hand. It emerged from RL. So the breakthrough was really about RL finally working at scale on top of a strong base model.

Agents are the next step along the same line, but the environment gets much bigger. A reasoning model is still mostly thinking inside its own head: one question, a long internal process, one answer. An agent has to interact with the outside world over many steps. It searches, calls tools, writes and runs code, looks at the result, and decides what to do next. The feedback is delayed, the environment is noisy, and a task might take dozens or hundreds of turns. From an RL perspective, it goes from something close to a single-step bandit problem to a true multi-step decision problem. That's actually the classic RL setting, which is why people like me who've worked on RL for a long time find this stage very exciting.

So I'd describe it this way: chatbots gave us a model that can talk, reasoning models gave us a model that can think, and agents give us a model that can act. Each stage builds on the previous one. You can't do good agentic RL without a strong reasoning model underneath, and you can't get a good reasoning model without a strong pretrained base.

The challenges change at each stage, though. For agents, the bottleneck is less about the algorithm itself and more about infrastructure and environments. How do you run thousands of long, asynchronous rollouts efficiently? How do you build realistic environments and reward signals for open-ended tasks? A lot of the work now is systems engineering, which is why we put so much effort into building RL training systems. It's an evolution, but each step forces you to rebuild part of the stack.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a reasoning model thinking “inside its own head” with an agent interacting with the outside world, observing results, and deciding what to do next.

r002.rationale: It describes agents taking many steps and choosing what to do next, but does not clearly state that they can continue from an initial instruction without step-by-step human instructions.

r003.rationale: It describes chatbots as one-turn ask-and-answer systems and reasoning models as handling one question through a long internal process before producing one answer.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's more accurate to call it one continuous line than three separate steps, but the line isn't about model architecture, it's about how much of a task you're willing to hand over before you check the output.

With a chatbot, the unit of trust is one message. You ask, it answers, you read it, you decide. If it's wrong, the cost is that you wasted thirty seconds. So the model never really had to be reliable, it just had to be helpful on average.

Reasoning models stretched that unit. Now the model works for a while before it shows you anything, and you're trusting a chain of intermediate steps you'll probably never inspect. That only becomes acceptable once the model can actually catch its own mistakes mid-process, which is really what the RL work on reasoning bought us. It wasn't just "longer thinking," it was the model learning to verify itself well enough that you don't have to.

Agents stretch it again, from one answer to a whole sequence of actions in an environment where each step changes the state. And here the thing I keep stressing is that errors compound. A model that's right ninety-five percent of the time per step is fine for a chatbot and nearly useless for a twenty-step agent, because you've got almost even odds of a failure somewhere. So the capability that matters most for agents isn't raw intelligence, it's robustness, the ability to notice when you've gone off track and recover. That's a different objective than what the earlier stages were optimizing.

So yes, iterative, in the sense that each stage was built on the previous one and used mostly the same ingredients: pretraining, then RL. But I'd resist the idea that it was inevitable or linear. Each transition required solving a specific problem that the previous stage could ignore. For reasoning it was reliable self-verification. For agents it's long-horizon credit assignment and environments that are good enough to learn from. If you look at what's actually hard in agent research right now, almost none of it is "make the model smarter." It's "make the feedback signal good enough that the model can learn to behave well over long horizons." That's a scaling problem, but it's a different axis of scaling than people usually mean.

r001.rationale: It describes agent actions changing the environment and the need for useful feedback, but does not clearly distinguish external-environment feedback from attending only to the agent’s own outputs.

r002.rationale: It says agents perform a sequence of actions, but does not state that they can continue pursuing an instruction without step-by-step human instructions.

r003.rationale: It says reasoning models work internally before showing an answer, but does not clearly state that they retain the chatbot’s human–machine turn-taking structure.

astra-6.text:
Yes, broadly speaking, I see it as an iterative evolution, although those three terms describe slightly different things. A chatbot is a way of interacting with a model. Reasoning is a capability: can the model work through a difficult problem, check its assumptions, and revise its approach? An agent is a system that uses capabilities like that to take actions and make progress toward a goal.

So these stages build on one another. A model that can reason more reliably can potentially make a better agent, because it can plan what to do and interpret the results. But reasoning alone doesn’t give you a reliable agent. Once you take action, you have to deal with feedback from the environment, mistakes, and situations you didn’t anticipate.

That’s where the challenge changes. In a conversation, you might produce a useful answer in one turn. As an agent, you need to keep making good decisions over many steps. A small error early on can affect everything that follows. So I would call it a continuous evolution in capability, with a substantial engineering challenge as we move from answering questions to carrying out tasks.

r001.rationale: The response says agents take actions and must handle feedback from the environment, contrasting this with producing a useful answer in one conversational turn.

r002.rationale: It says an agent makes progress toward a goal, but does not state that it can continue interacting with the environment from an initial instruction without step-by-step human guidance.

r003.rationale: It describes reasoning as a capability and chatbots as an interaction style, but does not state that reasoning models retain chatbot-style human–machine turn-taking while doing multiple internal steps before replying.

sol-6.1.text:
Yes, I think there’s a clear continuity, although I wouldn’t describe it as a simple sequence where each stage replaces the previous one. Chatbots give us a way to interact with models through language. Reasoning models improve the ability to work through problems that require multiple steps. Agents take those capabilities and put them into a loop: observe what’s happening, decide what to do, take an action, and use the feedback to decide the next step.

The important change is that the model is no longer just producing an answer. It’s interacting with an environment, and its actions affect what happens next. That introduces challenges around reliability, learning from feedback, and knowing whether a task has actually been completed.

So yes, it’s an iterative evolution in terms of the underlying technology. But moving toward agents also changes what we ask the system to do—and how we measure whether it’s doing it well.

r001.rationale: The response says agents observe the environment, act, and use feedback to decide the next step, distinguishing this loop from simply producing an answer.

r002.rationale: It describes agents taking further actions, but does not say they pursue an initial instruction without step-by-step human directions.

r003.rationale: It says reasoning models handle multistep problems, but does not state that they retain chatbot-style human–machine turn-taking while doing internal reasoning before replying.
